summary.text:
A tidy annual strategy from a small HRA-heavy authority. Total CFR £334.5m at 31.3.2025 rises to £377.4m by 2026/27, with HRA carrying 81% of it. External debt is £271.1m at 31.12.2025 — of which PWLB £247.987m has not moved since 31 March, and the paper flags a £12M January 2026 drawing to refinance HRA internal borrowing (after the reporting date). Under-borrowed by £63.2m at 31 March 2025, the paper is honest that this position closes over the plan (§4.11.1 shows it narrowing to £20.6m by 2028/29 as external borrowing catches up) and §4.7.4 concedes 'the Council will need to externally borrow to replace internal borrowing in the medium term'.

The book is dominated by the 2012 HRA self-financing pool — £194.911m of the £246.231m HRA PWLB — priced at rates that would look attractive today. Our file places 14 tranches of that pool weighted at 3.34% maturing between 2028 and 2041, with the whole book (28 loans, £259.5m) inside a 25-year horizon and weighted around 3.4%. Against 14 August curves (notice 314/26 PM) 27 of 28 loans sit below par; net indicative discount is around £25.76m or 9.9% of principal — a scale that is a live consideration if surplus cash appears (§5.4.1). Loan-book totals reconcile within £500k of the paper's £247.987m; not a clean tie, so the loan-book claim is left out of the email per PIPELINE guidance.

The published rate view is testable. MUFG's 9 January 2026 forecast (§4.13.1) had Bank Rate at 3.75% falling to 3.25% by Q4 2026, and the 25-year PWLB Standard falling from 5.80% at end-March to 5.30% by Sep 2027. On 14 August the curve sits about 0.85 points higher across all tenors than that Mar-26 starting point (5Y Cert 5.34%, 10Y 5.83%, 25Y 6.46%, 50Y 6.27%), and Bank Rate is still 3.75% — MUFG's Q2 2026 cut has not happened. §5.2.1 argues 'medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels'; five months on the direction has not turned. That, together with the Liability Benchmark converging to zero by 2028 — which mechanically implies externalising ~£13m of internal borrowing over the next two years — is the shape of the interesting story for members.

Investments earned an unusual 5.27% for FY-to-31.12.25 (£1.8M interest on portfolio ~£46-56m); §5.8.1 budgets a fall to 3.5% in 2026/27, with the weighted rate on debt rising as new draws replace historic cheap money. No LOBO holdings; LOBOs and the UK National Wealth Fund both on the Appendix E approved list as permissible future sources.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts ahead of your mid-year treasury report. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your annual strategy is clearly laid out and the identities all rebuild against each other — 334.475 less 254.057 less 17.235 comes back to the £63.183m of internal borrowing on page 12 — and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The part worth surfacing is dated and testable. MUFG's forecast in your section 4.13.1 was dated 9 January and had Bank Rate at 3.75% falling to 3.25% by Q4 2026, and the 25-year PWLB Standard falling from 5.80% at end-March to 5.30% by September 2027 — with the borrowing stance at 5.2.1 built explicitly on the view that 'medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels'. On 14 August the PWLB Certainty curve is 5-year 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, 25-year 6.46% and 50-year 6.27%. Against MUFG's Mar-26 starting point that's about 0.85 higher across every tenor, and against the Sep-27 endpoint they were pencilling in for a year from now it's 1.3 to 1.4 higher. Bank Rate is still 3.75% — the Q2 2026 cut has not happened. That doesn't invalidate the forecast, and forecasts are meant to be revisited; it dates the reference point, and members may find it useful to see what the curve has done since the strategy was signed off.

The reason that matters for Stevenage specifically is in your own liability benchmark. Your section 4.7 (over)/under table shows the Council over-borrowed against benchmark by £13.65m in 2026 and £12.38m in 2027, converging to essentially zero by 2028 — which mechanically implies externalising broadly that amount of internal borrowing across the next two years. 4.7.4 says the same in words: 'the Council will need to externally borrow to replace internal borrowing in the medium term'. Under-borrowing was £63.183m at 31 March 2025 and your 4.11.1 table shows the position closing to £20.617m by 2028/29. So the pace at which the curve moves matters for the timing of that.

Alongside that, the composition is unusual and worth naming. About £194.9m of your £247.987m PWLB — the 2012 HRA self-financing pool listed at section 5.1.4 — sits between 2027 and 2040 at rates well below anything available today. Your section 5.4.1 keeps rescheduling on the table 'whilst premature redemption rates remain elevated but only if there is surplus cash available' — the whole book is deeply below par at today's DMO premature rates. That's not a recommendation, and I'd rather understate it than overstate it: we hold no LOBO, no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled, whether anything is worth doing turns on replacement cost and cash timing we don't model, and only the DMO can quote a binding settlement. But the shape is knowable: the average life of your book, priced against today's rates, and the size of the below-par position are all things we surface daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. It is a lens on the £5.4.1 sentence, not an answer to it.

The monthly PWLB activity board at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the counterpart to the rates page: July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, after the thinnest May in years. That helps see whether the market is thinning or reopening before you time an externalisation, not after. And the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes about ten seconds to check at either fixing.

On training, four fit Stevenage well. Interest rate risk maps directly to the 5.2.1 assumption. Strategic PWLB borrowing addresses the sequencing of the ~£13m externalisation implied by your liability benchmark. HRA treasury & self-financing speaks to the 2012 pool that dominates the book. And our Liability Benchmark: using it in practice is interactive, built on live data, and worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
